title: Balisto's Electric Farm Machine Targets India's Labour Shortage for Small Farmers
excerpt: Mumbai-based Balisto Agritech's 130 Pro combines weeding, rotavating and trolley work in one electric unit priced from Rs 2.5 lakh, as the Tech30 startup tries to scale beyond its first 30 customers.
body:
• Mumbai-based Balisto Agritech, founded in 2024, sells the Balisto 130 Pro, an electric multi-purpose machine for small farms.
  • The machine handles earthing up, weeding, intercultivation, rotavating and trolley work, using detachable batteries and three motors.
  • Prices in the source are Rs 2.5 lakh for a single-battery version and Rs 3 lakh for a double-battery version, sold through dealers in Maharashtra.
  • The company says more than 30 machines have been sold, used across more than 600 acres, with a target of more than 200 sales by March 2027.

A Mumbai-based startup is trying to replace a mix of manual labour, bullocks and several diesel machines with one electric unit. Balisto Agritech's Balisto 130 Pro, profiled in YourStory's Tech30 cohort, is designed to work across the crop cycle on small plots where hiring labour has become harder and diesel costs remain a burden.

The problem the company describes is familiar across Indian agriculture: farm work is labour-intensive, fewer young people want to do it, and smallholders often need a different machine for each job. Balisto's answer is a single multi-purpose electric machine rather than a fleet.

What the machine does

According to YourStory, every machine sold today can be used for earthing up, weeding, intercultivation, rotavating and trolley operations. It runs on detachable batteries and can be controlled from an electric dashboard or by remote control.

At the centre is a control unit running company-developed firmware. It manages the battery and three motors — one for each wheel and one for the rotary unit at the back. Separate motors let the system correct the machine's line or speed as it moves. Each unit also sends data over an internet connection to company servers, allowing remote fault diagnosis.

A separate company listing describes the 130 Pro as a next-generation electric power tiller built for Indian farms, and lists dealer and field roles across Maharashtra districts including Beed, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Satara, Sangli, Kolhapur, Pandharpur and Jalgaon, consistent with a dealer-led sales model. See the Balisto Agritech listing for that regional footprint.

Founders and route to market

Balisto was founded in 2024 by IIT Bombay alumni Aishwarya Ramakrishnan and Kedar Gokhale, who later worked together at Boston Consulting Group. Ramakrishnan also holds an MBA from Harvard Business School and previously worked at the Mahindra Group, including on its agritech venture Krish-e. Gokhale previously ran an agritech startup and later led delivery-fleet operations at Swiggy.

The company took 18 to 20 months from prototype to commercial rollout, selling an initial batch to paying farmers for feedback along the way. Last year it sold 15 earlier-version machines at introductory prices across four districts and eight crops. It says total sales now exceed 30 machines, with cumulative sales since June 2025 crossing Rs 60 lakh, and that customers have used the machines across more than 600 acres, saving an estimated 3,300 litres of diesel. The current version is described as government-certified, subsidy-eligible and patented.

Machines are sold through multi-brand dealers in Maharashtra, who handle sales and after-sales service. Manufacturing is at a plant in Pimpri-Chinchwad, Pune, with capacity for 60 units a month, scalable to 150, and a team of more than 40 people.

Price and what comes next

The single-battery version costs Rs 2.5 lakh and the double-battery version Rs 3 lakh, with a three-year battery warranty, YourStory reported. Those figures matter because the pitch only works if a small farmer can recover the cost against hired labour and diesel over a few seasons — a calculation that will vary sharply by crop, acreage and local wage rates.

Balisto says an autonomous version is in advanced research and development, using the same hardware with a magnetometer and GPS added. It plans to add autonomy and more multi-purpose features this financial year, aims to sell more than 200 machines by March 2027 and targets profitability within three years. Its pre-seed round in April-May 2024 came from micro venture firms, family offices and angel investors; the amount was not disclosed, and the funds went mainly to research, product development and manufacturing.

The test now is scale: dealer service quality, battery life in real field conditions and resale of the savings claim beyond the first 30 customers will decide whether the 130 Pro becomes a standard small-farm tool or stays a promising early product.
